The preference itself comes from 27/8, which makes DEPA-registered goods promoted supplies, and 27/9 on direct or selective purchase. 27/8 should be added.

Clause 73 just extends the international-tender procedure of clause 60 (Thai or English documents, 30 business days' notice) to international price comparisons. That helps foreign bidders rather than limiting them, and it is also an English copy of the Thai clause 73. The consultant rule intended here is section 73 of the Act.
This is the English translation of section 73, which we are approving in the Thai Gazette text for this same indicator. Only the Thai text has legal force, so this copy is rejected as a duplicate.

Section 73 lets only consultants registered with the MoF Consultants Information Centre tender for state work, unless the Centre certifies that no registered consultant offers the service. Since registration turns on Thai nationality or majority Thai ownership, this is a genuine bidding limitation, and it equally supports a foreign-exclusion reading: outsiders get in only when no registered consultant exists.

Clause 73 applies the international-procurement steps of clause 60, English-language documents and a longer notice period, to international price comparisons. It widens foreign access and restricts nobody, so it doesn't answer the limitation question. The consultant-registration rule is section 73 of the Act, not this clause.

Clause 4(1) requires an independent consultant to be a Thai national to register, and section 73 of the Act makes registration the ticket to tender, ICT consultancy included. That is a nationality-based bidding limitation, and with section 73 it also supports a foreign-exclusion reading. Clause 7 still lets foreigners permitted to work or do business in Thailand register.

Sub-item (2) sets degree and years-of-experience requirements that every applicant must meet, Thai or foreign. That is an ordinary competence test, not a preference; the only nationality element in clause 4 is sub-item (1), which we already hold.

Sub-item (3) bars someone who is a managing director or a full-time employee elsewhere, a conflict-of-interest condition that applies to everyone. It gives Thai bidders no advantage; the nationality rule is sub-item (1), already held.
Excluding applicants who are serving a final prison sentence is a neutral character requirement, and the nationality limb of clause 4 is already covered under sub-item (1).
Disqualifying persons of unsound mind or without legal capacity, as sub-item (5) does, applies to every applicant and has nothing to do with foreign suppliers, so only the 4(1) entry should stay.

Sub-item (6) imports the general eligibility conditions of section 64 of the Act, such as legal capacity and not being bankrupt or blacklisted, which bind Thai and foreign consultants alike. It adds no preference or restriction beyond what sub-item (1) already shows.

Section 101 deals with appointing and paying a supervisor for staged construction works. It says nothing about who may bid. The foreign-consultant rule this was meant to capture is clause 101 of the MoF Regulation, which we are approving separately.

This is the English version of section 101, the construction-supervisor provision, so it fails for the same reason as the Thai text: it has nothing to do with bidding. It is also only a copy of the Thai Gazette text, which governs.

Paragraph two lets an agency hire a foreign consultant only after recording why it is necessary, and then requires Thai personnel on the team for knowledge transfer unless the field has none. Those burdens fall only on foreign consultants, so this is a nationality-based limitation; the necessity test also backs the exclusion reading of section 73.

All clause 12 does is declare Thai Innovation List goods to be promoted supplies. The rule that actually favours them, the 30% budget floor with direct or selective purchasing, is clause 13, and that is the evidence to use; clause 12 adds nothing on its own.

Clause 3 lists farm produce from named state bodies and royal projects, such as school milk, rice and seed, as promoted supplies. It has no bearing on ICT goods or foreign bidders. The Thai Innovation List reservation sometimes attributed to this clause is in clause 13, and it is 30%, not 70%.
Item (1) is school milk from the Dairy Farming Promotion Organization, an agricultural supply with no ICT or foreign-bidder angle.
Item (2) covers Chitralada UHT milk and other royal-project products. It is a food-purchasing preference unrelated to digital trade, and it repeats the clause 3 entry.
Rice seed from a government department is an agricultural promoted supply. It does not touch ICT procurement or foreign suppliers.
Item (7) favours handicrafts, tissue-culture plants and food products of the Mae Fah Luang Foundation. Nothing in it concerns ICT goods, digital services or foreign bidders.

The new clause 7(1) lets agencies buy directly from village groups, cooperatives, the veterans' organisation, disability organisations, prisons and social enterprises, or tender openly instead. It is an optional social-procurement route with no quota, margin, nationality test or ICT focus. The SME set-aside and 10% margin are in clause 7(2), not here.

This is the same optional direct-purchase route for community, welfare and social-enterprise producers as the clause 3 entry. It is a duplicate and, in any case, not a bidding limitation that affects foreign ICT suppliers.

Clause 13 obliges agencies to spend at least 30% of the relevant budget on Thai Innovation List goods and services, buying directly or by selection among listed sellers. That is a budget reservation for listed suppliers, ICT products included. It is status-based on its face and becomes nationality-based only through the list's 51% Thai-shareholding criterion, which sits outside this Regulation.
Sub-item (1) only tells agencies to buy directly when a listed item has a single seller. It is part of the clause 13 reservation we are already approving, so a separate entry duplicates it.
Selective tendering among all listed sellers, sub-item (2), is the procedural half of the clause 13 reservation. It adds nothing beyond the clause 13 entry and should be dropped as a duplicate.

Clause 27 lets agencies hire the food-safety and farm-product laboratory services of clause 26 directly, or tender them openly if they prefer. It is an optional direct-award route for named testing bodies, with no ICT dimension and no rule about foreign bidders.

A chapter title announcing 'domestic production promotion supplies' imposes nothing. The Made-in-Thailand rules that do, including the 60% domestic-content floor and the 3% margin for Thai bidders, are in clause 27/3.

These are definitions: Made-in-Thailand supplies (goods certified by the Federation of Thai Industries) and what counts as using imported goods. They create no preference by themselves; cite 27/1 alongside 27/3, where the obligations are.

On its own, clause 27/2 only makes FTI-listed Made-in-Thailand goods promoted supplies. What bites on bidders, the Made-in-Thailand purchase default, the 60% domestic-content floor and the 3% margin, is all in clause 27/3, which should carry this evidence.
This is the same passage, word for word, as the 27/3(3) entry carrying the 3% margin and the 60% content floor. One entry is enough; keep the more precise 27/3(3) pinpoint.

As quoted, this just duplicates the 27/3(3) entry. The real item (1), which makes Made-in-Thailand goods the default and allows imports only on shortage, too few bidders or necessity with higher approval, deserves separate evidence and arguably bears on foreign exclusion too.
The quoted text duplicates the 27/3(3) entry. Item (2) itself covers only materials for construction works, outside ICT procurement, so it would add nothing here even if quoted correctly.

Item (3) requires non-construction hires to use at least 60% Made-in-Thailand materials or equipment, and the next paragraph awards the contract to a Thai national or Thai-incorporated bidder within 3% of the lowest foreign bid. That margin turns on nationality and place of incorporation, so it discriminates directly against foreign bidders, ICT service contracts included.

This defines green goods and services by life-cycle impact. It is an environmental purchasing criterion open to any product, local or imported, and gives no edge based on a bidder's nationality, origin or size.

Products on the Pollution Control Department's green list become promoted supplies under clause 27/5. A foreign product can qualify as readily as a Thai one, so this origin-neutral environmental preference doesn't restrict foreign bidders.

The quoted clause 31 lets agencies hire state universities as consultants directly, provided the university's own staff lead the project and make up 80% of the team. That conditions a preference for public universities; it is not a limitation on private or foreign bidders, and the label is wrong.

The 80% own-staff rule binds state universities that take consultancy work through the direct-hire route. It is a condition on a public-body preference, not a bidding limitation on foreign firms, and it repeats the 27/6 entry.
A duplicate of the 27/6(1) entry that fails for the same reason: the staffing condition applies to public universities hired directly, and it neither favours Thai bidders nor restricts foreign ones.

Clause 27/9 lets agencies buy DEPA-registered digital goods and services directly from a sole seller, or by selection among registered sellers, instead of open tender. The Gazette note says the aim is Thailand's own digital operators. It is discretionary and DEPA's registration criteria are unverified, so treat it as status-based rather than proven nationality discrimination.
The sole-seller direct purchase in sub-item (1) is already covered by the 27/9 entry we are approving. A second entry for the same text adds nothing.
Selective tendering among registered sellers is part of the same 27/9 channel we are accepting. Drop this as a duplicate.

Clause 3B(a) allows only Class-I local suppliers to bid in multi-award tenders for items a nodal ministry has notified as having enough local capacity. Imported goods are shut out of those categories, so it works as a category exclusion; it bites only where such a notification exists, as with DoT's 2024 telecom list.

This makes documents produced for the project the department's property and bars the provider from keeping or releasing them. It is a work-product and confidentiality clause; it does not require a cloud provider to hand over its source code, patents or trade secrets.

The government 'shall endeavour' to prefer open-source over closed-source software. That is a best-efforts technology preference any supplier, foreign or Indian, can meet; it sets no price margin, set-aside or local-content condition tied to who the bidder is.

This paragraph only makes suppliers self-certify on Form-1 that their items meet the minimum local content and say where value is added. It is the paperwork behind the local-content rule; the limitation itself is the Table-A thresholds and the Class-I requirement, which should be cited instead.

Paragraph 14 treats any bidder offering imported products as a non-local supplier and stops it counting transport, installation, training or maintenance as local value. It decides who gets the Make in India advantage by product origin, so it is part of the discriminatory local-content regime for telecom procurement.

In multi-award tenders, the lowest Class-I local supplier within 20% of the lowest price gets first right to supply. That is a price preference based on local content that still lets foreign bidders win, so it belongs under bidding limitations.

Clause 3A(a) is the general rule that procuring entities 'shall' give purchase preference to Class-I local suppliers, with the 20% margin set in clause 2 and the award mechanics in 3A(b) to (d). It is the core domestic-preference provision in Indian government buying.
Same domestic-capability rule as the current Article 63(2), which we are keeping from the 2025 text. This older copy under the wrong paragraph number should go.
A superseded repeat of the below-threshold rule. The 2025 wording is the one to rely on.
Repeats Article 63(2) from the old text. The exclusion is already recorded from Perpres 46/2025, so this adds nothing.
The rule is the heart of the foreign exclusion, but it should be evidenced from the current 2025 wording, which we hold. Retire this 2018 version.

Paragraph (3) makes foreign firms in international tenders team up with Indonesian firms. They can still win through a consortium or subcontract, so this limits bidding rather than excluding anyone, and it is old text besides.

Article 61(1) requires domestic products where one reaches a combined TKDN and company-benefit score of 40%. A foreign supplier can meet that with Indonesian-made goods, so it is a local-content limitation, and it is already accepted as such.

Allowing imports only when goods cannot be made locally, or not in enough volume, is the tail end of the local-content regime. A foreign firm can still win by supplying Indonesian-made goods, so this does not bar foreign firms; the exclusion rests on Article 63(2).

Article 57 lists who must use domestic products: government bodies spending budget money, and state and private firms in budget-funded or partnership work. It sets the reach of a local-content rule, not a ban on foreign bidders, and it is already accepted under bidding limitations.
A general duty to use domestic products is a local-content rule, not an exclusion of foreign firms, and this wording has been superseded in any case.
This is the core TKDN threshold. It restricts foreign-made goods, not foreign firms, and leaves a route to win with local products, so it belongs with the bidding limitations.

The duty to buy domestic products, with imports only as a fallback under paragraph (4), can be met by any supplier offering local goods. It is not a foreign exclusion, and the paragraph is mislabelled as well.

Article 66 sets up the TKDN cascade and allows imports only at the end of it. That governs the origin of goods and is open to anyone offering Indonesian-made products, so it evidences a limitation, where it is already held, not an exclusion.
Paragraph (1) is a general instruction to use domestic products. It does not stop a foreign firm from bidding; its proper place is the local-content limitation already taken from this article.
A further copy of the 2018 Article 63(2). Keep only the 2025 version.
Article 58(1) only says the domestic-product duty applies at the planning and execution stages. It is procedural and excludes no one.
Duplicate of Article 63(2) in its superseded form; it offers nothing beyond the 2025 text we already hold.
A TKDN-plus-benefit threshold decides which goods qualify, not which firms may bid, and this is the superseded wording.
Duplicate of the Article 63(2) passage already accepted from the same 2025 text, here under the wrong paragraph.

Read with the definition in Article 1(38), foreign firms may compete only in International Procurement, which paragraph (1) limits to large contracts (above Rp50 billion for goods and other services). Below that, paragraph (2) opens it only where no capable Indonesian business exists: a 'foreign only if locals cannot supply' rule, and a genuine exclusion.
Yet another copy of the below-threshold rule from the old text. Remove it; the 2025 Article 63(2) is the evidence.
The import fallback is part of the local-content regime, not a firm-level exclusion, and this version has been superseded.
A truncated repeat of the old import-fallback clause, which in any event goes to the origin of goods rather than excluding foreign firms.
A third copy of the old import-fallback clause. It does not bar foreign firms and should be dropped.
Article 16 sets up the teams that run self-managed (swakelola) procurement and has nothing to do with foreign suppliers. ESCAP's reference to 'reg. 16' is the regulation number, not this article.
Paragraph (2) lists the preparation team's planning tasks for in-house work. It is irrelevant to whether foreign firms can bid.
The implementation team's recording and reporting duties in self-managed procurement say nothing about foreign participation.

Article 58 limits the written warning for SNI certification bodies, labs and inspectors to one warning with 15 days to put things right. It has no connection with procurement; the Articles 57, 58, 61 and 64 in ESCAP's note are PP 29/2018 provisions.
Paragraph (2)'s 25% minimum TKDN is a local-content floor. It shapes what goods can be offered, not who may bid.
Another copy of Article 61(1), which is a local-content threshold rather than an exclusion.
Duplicate of paragraph (1), and under the wrong heading: a TKDN threshold limits bids, it does not exclude foreign firms.
A fourth copy of Article 61(1) under the exclusion heading. The threshold is recorded once, as a limitation.

Article 64 lets the government fix production volumes, distribution and prices for strategic industries. It is an industrial-policy control, not a procurement rule, and says nothing about foreign bidders.

Article 4(2) requires the local-content share of a telecom operator's network spending to be validated by an authorised body. It concerns licensed operators' own commercial purchases, not government tenders, so it is a commercial local-content rule outside procurement.

Article 6 counts a telecom component with at least 50% local content as fully local when operators calculate their TKDN. That is a measurement rule for the commercial telecom market and keeps no foreign firm out of government tenders.

Article 86(1) obliges state bodies to use domestic products when buying with state or regional budget money. A foreign supplier can meet that with goods made in Indonesia, and paragraph (4) relaxes it where local products are unavailable, so it is a local-content limitation, not a bar on foreign firms.

Paragraph (3) requires contractors to use domestic or small-business materials and equipment during performance, as promised in their bids. It controls which goods are used, not who may tender, so at most it is a local-content condition under bidding limitations.

Paragraph (1a) tells the commitment official to pitch domestic-product specifications at what Indonesian industry can supply, using the Ministry of Industry inventory. It is a drafting instruction, and paragraph (3) applies the domestic preference only 'as far as available'; nothing here stops a foreign firm from tendering.

Article 9(1) obliges developers of software built specifically for public-scope system operators, that is government bodies, to hand over the source code and documentation, with third-party escrow under paragraphs (3) and (4). It attaches to every such government software contract, so it is a source-code surrender condition.
Duplicates the Article 9(1) hand-over duty already accepted. If the escrow guarantee is wanted as separate support, extract the actual text of paragraph (4).
Same source-code duty as Article 9(1); there is no need to record it twice.
A repeat of paragraph (1). Paragraph (5) itself, a confidentiality obligation on the agency, would not be a surrender condition anyway.
Duplicate of the Article 9(1) hand-over rule; paragraph (2) binds the agency, not the supplier.
Another repeat of Article 9(1) under a different paragraph number. Drop it.

Article 8 only requires software used by system operators to be secure, reliable and able to sustain service. It demands no source code, IP or encryption from suppliers; ESCAP's note describes the source-code rule, which was Article 8 of PP 82/2012 and is now Article 9.
Article 15(1) is the right to have irrelevant personal information erased. It is a data-protection right with no bearing on procurement or source code.
Paragraph (3) identifies which operators must honour erasure requests. That is privacy law, not a tender condition.
Article 10 governs what telecom operators must attach to their annual TKDN reports. It is a reporting rule for the commercial telecom sector, not a limitation on government bidding.

The new Article 65 requires agencies to buy Indonesian-made products of micro and small firms and cooperatives, to spend at least 40% of their goods and services budget on them, and reserves packages up to Rp15 billion for those firms. These set-asides turn on size and domestic origin, a clear bidding limitation.
An obsolete small-business set-aside. The current reservation is taken from the 2025 Article 65.

Article 15(3) says how to count level-three industrial services when calculating a service's TKDN. It is a certification formula, not a preference or threshold in tendering; the procurement effect comes from PP 29/2018 and the procurement Perpres.
The partnering duty is a real limitation, but it is recorded from the current 2025 text. This older, mislabelled copy is redundant.
Allowing international contracts to be paid in rupiah or as the law permits is a payment rule, not a preference, quota or set-aside.
Duplicate of the consortium requirement, already taken from the 2025 text.
Another old copy of the partnering duty. Keep only the current version.
Tracing a service's inputs back to level-two domestic suppliers is part of the TKDN arithmetic. It does not itself prefer or reserve anything in a government tender.
Duplicate of the consortium duty already accepted from the same article.
Paragraph (3) treats components an operator cannot document as foreign in its own TKDN self-assessment. It regulates telecom operators' commercial network spending, not government procurement.
The obsolete Rp2.5 billion set-aside; the current one is in the 2025 Article 65(3).

Foreign firms entering international procurement must partner with an Indonesian firm by consortium, subcontract or similar arrangement. The duty is triggered purely by nationality yet still lets the foreign firm win, so it is a discriminatory limitation on bidding rather than an exclusion.

Article 63 lets signatories deposit their e-signature creation data only with Indonesian certification providers. That is a trust-services rule for electronic signatures, not a condition of government tendering.

This only says central government issues business licences for strategic industries. The ownership test ESCAP describes, requiring domestic service companies to be more than 50% Indonesian-owned, is Article 63 of PP 29/2018, which should be extracted instead.
Article 17 leaves the calculation of industrial-service TKDN to the Secretary-General. That is administrative machinery only.

Paragraph (1) says producers with R&D ('brainware') capacity may be given extra TKDN value. It is a discretionary certification uplift used for every TKDN purpose, not an evaluation bonus written into procurement law.
The 20% figure only sizes the brainware uplift on the TKDN certificate. It is certification arithmetic and duplicates the paragraph (1) extract.
Article 3 merely lists what TKDN is calculated for: goods, industrial services and combinations of the two. A scope clause in a certification regulation is not a procurement limitation.
Even in full, Article 4(1) is the weighting formula for goods TKDN. The procurement preference and thresholds come from other instruments.
Duplicates the paragraph (3) extract and, like it, is only a TKDN counting rule.
Requiring industrial-service activities to fall within the licensed business classification before TKDN can be calculated is an eligibility rule for certification, not for bidding.
Operators must report their self-assessed TKDN to the Director General within three months of year end. That is a reporting duty for commercial telecom operators, not a procurement rule.
Paragraph (2) only prescribes the report format. Nothing in it touches government tenders.
The substance is sound, but the partnering duty is already accepted from its current wording; this 2018 version should not be scored.
The 2025 amendment replaced this wording; paragraph (4) now also covers other services and says 'including but not limited to' spare parts and after-sales.
Duplicate of the consortium duty, which is held from the current text.
Yet another copy of Article 63(3); drop it.
A superseded set-aside, duplicated several times over from the same paragraph.
Old small-business reservation; the 2025 Article 65 carries the current one.
The small-business set-aside is a real limitation, but this figure is out of date and the current rule is already accepted from the 2025 text.
Another copy of the outdated Rp2.5 billion reservation.

Buyers covered by Article 57 must give a price preference to domestic products with at least 25% TKDN, capped at 25% for goods, and paragraph (3) lets domestic construction firms win at up to 7.5% above the lowest foreign bid. This is a mandatory, origin-based price preference in government purchasing.

Where a domestic product scores at least 40% on TKDN plus company benefit, covered buyers must use domestic products, and paragraph (2) requires at least 25% TKDN. That is a binding local-content threshold in public purchasing.
The local-content duty is held from the 2025 Article 66; this old version should not be scored.
Duplicate of Article 61(1), which is already accepted.
The same paragraph as the Article 66 extract we are keeping for bidding limitations; one copy is enough.

Article 57 places the duty to use domestic products on government bodies spending budget money and on state and private firms in budget-funded, partnership or state-resource purchasing. Read with the thresholds in Article 61, it is an operative local-content requirement open to any supplier of Indonesian-made goods.
Old wording of the local-content trigger; the current Article 66 is already held.

Article 66 obliges agencies to use domestic products and, for industrial goods, sets a cascade that starts with products of at least 25% TKDN wherever one reaching 40% TKDN plus company benefit exists, with imports only as a last resort. It is a local-content requirement any supplier of Indonesian-made goods can meet.
Repeats Article 61(1). If the 25% floor in paragraph (2) is wanted on its own, extract its actual text.
Paragraph (1) only fixes when the domestic-product duty applies, at planning and execution. The limitation itself is in Articles 57 and 61, which we hold.

Article 328 tells government and health facilities to give priority to medicines and medical devices made from domestic raw materials. It is a general priority for health products with no margin, quota or threshold attached, and it does not reach ICT goods or digital services.

The 40% target for Indonesian-made micro, small and cooperative products is an instruction to ministers and regional heads. The same allocation is now binding in Articles 20(3) and 65(2) of the procurement Perpres as amended in 2025, and those provisions should carry it.

Item 11 asks officials to put a domestic and small-business product clause into 'all cooperation contracts'. It is addressed to government, sets no threshold or preference, and the binding contract rules are Articles 52(3) and 66 of the amended procurement Perpres.

Paragraph (6) gives national firms a 7.5% price preference over the lowest foreign bid in international construction tenders, plus 5% when they lead a consortium with a foreign firm. That is an openly nationality-based margin, but it covers construction only, so it should back up the TKDN-based preference for goods and other services in paragraph (3), which still needs extracting.

When packaging procurement, the commitment official must allocate at least 40% of the goods and services budget to Indonesian-made products of micro and small enterprises and cooperatives. A set-aside tied to both firm size and domestic origin is a bidding limitation.

This is the 2018 version, under which national construction firms got the preference in any tender. The current, narrower rule is taken from the 2025 Article 67(6), so this older text should not be relied on.

Paragraph (1) only defined what a price preference is; the margin and TKDN trigger were in later paragraphs. The operative rule today is Article 67(3) of the 2025 text (up to 25% for goods and other services with at least 25% TKDN), which should be added.

Article 43 asks central and regional government to prioritise products holding a Green Industry Certificate. It is an environmental purchasing policy with no margin, quota or threshold, and nothing in its terms turns on nationality or origin.

Art. 14(4)(1) requires any bid offering foreign-origin goods covered by a Government ban to be rejected and forbids single-source contracts for them. With Resolution No. 1875's ban list in force, this is the statutory rule that shuts foreign goods out of those categories.

Para 20 requires the notice for SME-only purchases to say that only small and medium businesses may bid. Foreign firms cannot qualify, but this reserves a share of purchasing rather than barring foreign suppliers from a category, so it is a bidding limitation; the same paragraph is already put forward on that basis.

Para 10 lists the grounds on which a state-owned company's request to buy foreign software for significant critical infrastructure must be refused. Sub-paragraph (е) refuses it whenever a registered Russian or EAEU program of the same class meets the requirements, and (б) refuses it for sanctioned right-holders. Foreign software gets in only where no domestic equivalent exists.

Art. 1296(1) is the general civil-law default that a commissioned program belongs to the customer unless the contract says otherwise. It covers all commissioning, not government tenders specifically, and the parties can agree otherwise, so it is not a compulsory surrender of IP as a condition of public contracts.

Where the state already owns a contract result, point 5 makes the contractor acquire rights from its staff and subcontractors, exclusive or by licence, for transfer to the state. It follows from ownership fixed in points 3 and 4 and does not make bidders hand over their own source code or trade secrets to bid or win.

Art. 110²(1) requires design-documentation and engineering-survey contracts to vest the exclusive rights in the results in the state. These are construction deliverables, not ICT goods or digital services, and the clause concerns ownership of commissioned work, not surrender of a supplier's existing code or know-how.

Art. 110¹(1) gives the state the exclusive right to use architectural and landscape works created under the contract for project documentation, and to reuse that documentation. It is an architecture and construction rule well outside ICT procurement, and says nothing about source-code or IP demands on technology suppliers.
A line in a repeal list imposes no preference or quota on anyone. If the minimum Russian-goods share is wanted, cite para 2 of Resolution No. 1875 and its Annex 3.

This sentence only requires competitive procurements reserved for small and medium businesses to be run electronically. The reservation and its size come from the Government's rules in Resolution No. 1352, which are the provisions that actually limit bidding.

Part 3³ requires designated customers' procurement plans to list innovative and high-tech products to be bought from small and medium businesses, in an annual volume the Government sets. The volume is fixed by Government resolution, not here, so this is planning machinery rather than the operative preference.

Art. 27(4) entitles penal-system enterprises, disabled persons' organisations, small businesses and socially oriented non-profits to the procurement advantages in Arts. 28 to 30. These are status-based preferences in public tenders; the price advantages and the small-business quota themselves sit in Arts. 28 to 30, which should be cited alongside.

Para 20 requires the notice for reserved procurements to state that only small and medium businesses may bid. SME status is open only to firms registered under Russian law with limited foreign ownership, so foreign suppliers are kept out of this share of purchasing. It is a set-aside that limits bidding.

Para 5¹ requires at least 20% of a customer's planned annual purchasing to go through procurements open only to small and medium businesses. That is a quota, and because SME status depends on Russian registration and caps foreign ownership, it works against foreign bidders.

Tender documents must require goods that domestic producers can supply to be bought from domestic manufacturers, under a list approved by the Government. Foreign goods are shut out where local supply exists, which is an exclusion rather than a margin. Its reach into ICT depends on that list, which covers only a few ICT-related items.

The data-sheet entry defaults to the procuring entity owning IP created by the services, but the entity may change it to 'No'. It covers only work produced under the contract, not a bidder's existing source code or trade secrets, so it is not a condition to surrender IP in order to win.

In works tenders, a bidder whose ultimate owner is a Mongolian citizen gets a notional 7.5% price reduction (8.7.2), and firms operating locally get 5% (8.7.1). The first is a nationality-based preference. It applies only to works contracts, so the goods margins in 8.4 to 8.6 matter more for ICT purchases.

Article 19(1) opens national open bidding only to local individuals and legal entities; foreign firms may take part only in international open bidding. That excludes foreign bidders from a whole category of tenders. ESCAP read Article 19 as showing openness and scored 0, which the text does not bear out; the value thresholds still need confirming.

Article 45 requires domestic preference for qualifying contractors and suppliers and leaves the conditions to regulations. On its own it is a principle, but clause 14 of Instruction 0477/MOF gives it effect with a 7.5% works margin and a 15% margin for Lao-made goods. Read together they are an operative origin-based preference.

In international open bidding for works and maintenance, a local bidder wins if its price is within 7.5% of a foreign bidder's. That is a price preference for local contractors. It is limited to works, but it is a real handicap for foreign bidders.

Bidding documents must state any preference for Lao-made goods and how origin is to be proved, and the supplier's nationality is irrelevant. This confirms the goods preference turns on where products are made, which still disadvantages imported goods.
In international open bidding, goods made in Laos are preferred over goods made abroad when bids are compared. This is the core origin-based preference behind Article 45 of the law.

Imported goods (Group C) have up to 15% of their CIP price added before they are compared with the best domestic bid. This is the margin itself and the clearest single piece of the Lao goods preference.

This clause only says bids are compared on the Incoterms basis set in the bidding documents when the preference applies. It is evaluation mechanics, not a preference in its own right; the measure is already captured by clauses 14.2.1 and 14.2.7.

Bids are grouped by origin, and Lao goods qualify for the preferred group only if local labour, materials and components make up at least 30% of the ex-works price. That 30% local-content threshold is part of the substance of the preference and is worth keeping.

Clause 14.2.5 only fixes the price basis for comparison: domestic bids include duties paid on inputs, imported bids are taken on CIP terms. It is a pricing convention rather than a limit on bidders and adds nothing beyond the margin in 14.2.7.

This is the comparison step: find the lowest bid in each group and award to a domestic group if it is cheapest. The preference only bites in 14.2.7, where the 15% is added, so this step should not be counted as a separate measure.

This part of the Overview restates Articles 86 to 88 of the Procurement Code. The binding preference is Article 86 itself, which we already hold. The Overview helps show how the margin is applied but should not be counted as a separate measure.

Non-national suppliers that meet a local-content test can get at most a 5% uplift, against up to 10% for national suppliers under Article 86, and foreign firms without local content get nothing. The gap turns on nationality, so this is a discriminatory preference in bid evaluation.

Contracting entities must give national suppliers, meaning Timorese citizens or firms over 50% Timorese-owned, an uplift of up to 10% in score or price in open tenders, restricted tenders and quotations. That is a mandatory nationality-based preference. Paragraph 2(b) is loosely worded, but the 2026 Regulation applies it by loading non-national prices.
